Microbial electrolysis cell simultaneously enhancing methanization and 
reducing hydrogen sulfide production in anaerobic digestion of 
sewage sludge 
Xiangyu Chen a,b, Benyi Xiao a,b,*, Xinyi Tang a,b, Chunlin Bian a,c, Junxin Liu a,b, Lin Li a,b 
a Research Center for Eco-Environmental Sciences, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, 100085, China 
b University of Chinese Academy of Science, Beijing, 100049, China 
c School of Civil Engineering, Inner Mongolia University of Technology, Hohhot, 010051, China   
H I G H L I G H T S  
G R A P H I C A L  A B S T R A C T  
• The effects of high applied voltages on 
MEC-AD of sewage sludge were studied. 
• Methanization enhancement and H2S 
production 
reduction 
was 
simulta­
neously realized. 
• High voltages (1.3 V and 1.6 V) created 
micro-aerobic condition for the AD. 
• High voltages increased the abundances 
of SOB and decreased those of SRB. 
• High voltages enhanced the hydro­
genotrophic methanogenesis.  
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Handling Editor: A ADALBERTO NOYOLA  
Keywords: 
Applied voltage 
Hydrogen sulfide production 
Methanization 
Microaeration 
Microbial electrolysis cell-assisted anaerobic 
digestion 
Sewage sludge 
A B S T R A C T   
The effects of microbial electrolysis cells (MECs) at three applied voltages (0.8, 1.3, and 1.6 V) on simultaneously 
enhancing methanization and reducing hydrogen sulfide (H2S) production in the anaerobic digestion (AD) of 
sewage sludge were studied. The results showed that the MECs at 1.3 V and 1.6 V simultaneously enhanced the 
methane production by 57.02 and 12.70% and organic matter removal by 38.77 and 11.13%, and reduced H2S 
production by 94.8 and 98.2%, respectively. MECs at 1.3 V and 1.6 V created a micro-aerobic conditions for the 
digesters with oxidation-reduction potential as −178~-232 mv, which enhanced methanization and reduced H2S 
production. Sulfur reduction, H2S and elemental sulfur oxidation occurred simultaneously in the ADs at 1.3 V and 
1.6 V. The relative abundances of sulfur-oxidizing bacteria increased from 0.11% to 0.42% and those of sulfur- 
reducing bacteria decreased from 1.24% to 0.33% when the applied voltage of MEC increased from 0 V to 1.6 V. 
Hydrogen produced by electrolysis enhanced the abundance of Methanobacterium and changed the methano­
genesis pathway.

1. Introduction 
Sewage sludge, an inevitable by-product of biological wastewater 
treatment, is hazardous and contains various toxic substances such as 
pathogens, heavy metals, and organic contaminants (Wu et al., 2020). 
These contaminants may cause significant pollution and human health 
risks without appropriate treatment and disposal (Xiao et al., 2020; 
Yakamercan et al., 2021). Anaerobic digestion (AD) is a traditional 
method for treatment of sewage sludge and has been widely applied in 
wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) worldwide (Di Capua et al., 
2020; Xiao et al., 2020). AD converts part of the organic matter in the 
sludge into biogas containing 60–70% methane, which is a promising 
renewable energy source. The biogas energy potential is one of the most 
attractive advantages of AD for minimizing sludge from WWTPs (Díaz 
et al., 2010). 
Although methane and carbon dioxide are its main constituents, 
biogas also contains significant quantities of undesirable compounds, 
such as hydrogen sulfide (H2S) whose concentration can reach 1.0% (v/ 
v) (Díaz et al., 2010; Krayzelova et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2020; Nguyen 
and Khanal, 2018). H2S is formed by the reduction of inorganic (such as 
sulfate) and organic sulfur-containing compounds (such as proteins) in 
AD, and is a harmful substance in biogas and a vexing problem for the 
AD of sewage sludge (Krayzelova et al., 2015). H2S must be removed 
before biogas is used as its concentration in biogas often exceeds the 
technical limits of energy technologies. H2S also causes corrosion, 
toxicity, and odor-associated problems. In the liquid phase, dissolved 
H2S can easily diffuse through the cell membrane into the cytoplasm, 
damaging methanogens, particularly acetotrophic methanogens (Kray­
zelova et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2020). In addition, H2S-reducing bac­
teria, namely, sulfur-reducing bacteria (SRB), have a higher growth rate, 
higher substrate affinity for acetate and hydrogen (H2), and outcompete 
methanogens, thereby resulting in low methane yield and high H2S 
content in biogas (Liu et al., 2018; Nguyen and Khanal, 2018). There­
fore, the presence of H2S and SRB in AD limit methane production. It is 
necessary to control SRB to reduce H2S production during the AD of 
sludge. 
Microaeration, that is, supplying small quantities of air or oxygen, is 
an effective method to scavenge H2S from biogas by oxidizing sulfide to 
elemental sulfur, riching sulfur oxidizing bacteria (SOBs), and inhibiting 
the growth of SRBs, except for Desulfovibrio aerotolerans (Díaz et al., 
2010; Krayzelova et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2018). 
Microaeration is regarded as a highly efficient, simple, and economically 
feasible technology for removing H2S from biogas (Díaz et al., 2010; 
Krayzelova et al., 2015). Moreover, microaeration can improve AD of 
sludge by promoting hydrolysis and acidification, preventing volatile 
fatty acids (VFAs) accumulation, increasing organic matter removal, 
enhancing biogas production, and stabilizing the overall digestion 
processs (Chen et al., 2020). In microaeration, hydrolytic and acidifying 
bacteria will consume the oxygen, decrease the oxidation-reduction 
potential around the methanogens, which protect the methanogens. 
Therefore, although methanogenesis is strictly anaerobic, the increasing 
oxidation-reduction potential in microaerobic condition created by 
microaeration can enhance methanization and increase methane pro­
duction (Fu et al., 2023). Microaeration can be performed by air/oxygen 
injection, electrolytic aeration, and natural aeration (leaving the tested 
configuration open with or without shaking) (Girotto et al., 2018; 
Krayzelova et al., 2015). Although air/oxygen injection is the most 
studied method, electrolytic aeration has unique advantages: the oxygen 
produced by electrolysis can create microaeration conditions, while the 
hydrogen produced by electrolysis can improve the combustion char­
acteristics of biogas and further increase the net production of methane 
(Tartakovsky et al., 2011). Additionally, electrolytic aeration can over­
come a drawback of air injection, namely, the dilution of biogas with 
nitrogen (Girotto et al., 2018). 
Microbial electrolysis cells (MEC) are a type of electrolysis cell that 
use electrochemically active bacteria to convert organic matter into 
hydrogen or a variety of by-products without polluting the environment 
at lower applied voltages (Hua et al., 2019). Recently, MEC-assisted AD 
(MEC-AD) has been investigated as a means of improving AD and 
increasing methane recovery (Yu et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2022). 
MEC-AD can accelerate the degradation of a substrate (including 
recalcitrant compounds) and alter the AD microbial community by 
enriching exoelectrogens and methanogens. In MEC-AD, exoelectrogens, 
such as Geobacter sulfurreducens and Shewanella oneidensis, anaerobically 
ferment organic matter to produce electrons, which is transferred to 
methanogens through direct electron transfer or direct interspecies 
electron transfer (DIET). When MEC was combined with AD, the suitable 
applied voltage of MEC can provide energy required for respiration of 
exoelectrogens and methanogens, enrich them, increase their activities, 
enhance DIET between them, conquer thermodynamics barriers there­
fore enhancing the organic acid degradation, promote H2 formation to 
enhance hydrogenoetrophic methanogenesis (Wang et al., 2022; Yu 
et al., 2018). Thereby, the AD was enhanced and methane production 
increased. Despite the theoretically minimum applied voltage of 0.14 V, 
most MEC-AD were operated at applied voltages of 0.3–1.5 V (Yu et al., 
2018; Wang et al., 2022). Applied voltages above 1.0 V (high voltage) 
are generally not recommended because the electrical energy input is so 
large that the microbial electrolysis process becomes similar to a water 
electrolysis process and may show negative effects (Yu et al., 2018; 
Wang et al., 2022). However, some studies have shown that appropri­
ately high applied voltages (>1.0 V) can also improve AD by creating 
microaerobic conditions through in situ electrolytic oxygen (Chen et al., 
2016; Ding et al., 2021; Tartakovsky et al., 2011; Xiao et al., 2018). For 
example, Tartakovsky et al. (2011) studied the effect of an applied 
voltage of 2.8–3.5 V on the AD of synthetic wastewater in MEC-up-flow 
anaerobic sludge bed and found that oxygen and hydrogen were pro­
duced by electrolysis, which created microaerobic conditions and 
enhanced methane production by 10–25%. Chen et al. (2016) found that 
the applied voltage of 1.2 V and 1.5 V increased the methane yield of 
waste-activated sludge AD by 40.5–51.6%, although this was lower than 
that of 0.6 V (76.2%). 
Since MEC-AD, at a suitable applied voltage can create microaerobic 
conditions, it is expected that it can reduce the H2S concentration in 
biogas. However, the effects of applied voltage on simultaneous 
methanization enhancement and H2S production reduction for MEC-AD 
have not been investigated, and the resultant environmental benefits 
have been neglected. Therefore, the objective of this study was to study 
the effect of applied voltage on methanization and H2S production in the 
MEC-AD of sewage sludge. 
2. Material and methods 
2.1. Sewage sludge and inoculum 
Sewage sludge used in the test was obtained from a WWTP in Beijing, 
China. Anaerobic digestate from an anaerobic digester in the same 
WWTP was used as the inoculum for AD. The characteristics of the 
sewage sludge and inoculum are summarized in Table 1. 
2.2. MEC-assisted anaerobic digesters 
The MEC-assisted anaerobic digesters were cylindrical plexiglass jars 
with two electrodes (Fig. S1). The volume of the digesters was 250 mL 
with a working volume of 180 mL. The electrodes were made of a cy­
lindrical carbon rod (length × diameter = 8 × 0.5 cm2) and four rect­
angular carbon felts (length × width × thickness = 2 × 1 × 0.5 cm3), 
with the carbon rod passing through the center of the carbon felts. The 
distance between the two adjacent carbon felts was 0.5 cm. The digesters 
had three ports for outgassing, liquid sampling, and oxidation-reduction 
potential (ORP) electrode.

2.3. Anaerobic digestion of sewage sludge 
Sewage sludge (120 mL) and the inoculum (60 mL) were added to 
each digester. The digesters were purged with nitrogen for 5 min to 
create an anaerobic environment prior to sealing. The digesters were 
then placed in a water bath shaker (120–130 RPM) and incubated at 37 
± 1 ◦C. The two electrodes of the digesters were connected to DC power 
supplies using wires. The voltages applied between the two electrodes 
were 0, 0.8, 1.2, and 1.6 V. The tests were conducted in triplicate, and 
the results are presented as the mean value. 
2.4. Analytical methods 
The biogas produced from the digesters was periodically measured 
by displacing a saturated aqueous NaCl solution (Guo et al., 2014). The 
methane content in the produced biogas was measured using a gas 
chromatograph (Agilent 6890 N, USA) equipped with a flame ionization 
detector and a 30 m capillary column (HP-5). The H2S content in the 
produced biogas was measured using another gas chromatograph 
(Agilent 6890, USA) equipped with a flame photometric detector and a 
30 m capillary column (DB-1701). 
Digestate pH was measured using a pH meter (Sartorius PB-10, 
Germany). The ORP of the digestate was measured in situ using a pH/ 
ORP meter (KP-10Z, Kasahara Chemical Instruments Co., Japan). The 
sulfate concentration in the digestate was measured by ion chromatog­
raphy (ICS-1000, Dionex, USA). The elemental sulfur on the electrodes 
was qualitatively analyzed using an elemental analyzer (Vario EL III, 
Germany). The soluble chemical oxygen demand (SCOD), total chemical 
oxygen demand (TCOD), soluble deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), total 
solids, and volatile solids (VS) of the sewage sludge, inoculum, and 
digestate were measured using standard methods (APHA, 2012). The 
scanning electron microscopy (SEM) of digestates at the end of AD was 
conducted using a scanning electron microscope (JEOL JSM-7610 F, 
Japan). 
2.5. Microbial analysis 
According to a previous study (Xiao et al., 2020), the digestates 
sampled from the digesters at the end of the test were used to analyze 
their microbial communities. The DNA extraction of digestates, poly­
merase chain reaction (PCR) amplification of the extracted DNA, and 
Illumina MiSeq sequencing of the amplicons were performed following 
the methodology used in a previous study (Xiao et al., 2020), and the 
detailed processes are summarized in Supplementary Material S1. The 
raw reads were deposited in the National Center for Biotechnology In­
formation (NCBI) Sequence Read Archive database (accession number: 
PRJNA883421). The sequencing data was processed as described in

3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Performances of anaerobic digestion 
The methane production of the four MEC-ADs is summarized in 
Fig. 1-A and B. At the end of the test, the cumulative methane production 
of the four MEC-ADs was 151 ± 10 mL (0 V), 223 ± 15 mL (0.8 V), 237 
± 13 mL (1.3 V), and 170 ± 14 mL (1.6 V) (Fig. 1-A). The three applied 
voltages enhanced the methane production of sludge by 47.62 ± 1.67% 
(0.8 V), 57.02 ± 1.71% (1.3 V), and 12.70 ± 0.55% (1.6 V) at the end of 
the test (Fig. 1-A). The enhancement in methane production in this study 
was similar to that reported in previous studies (Ding et al., 2016; Xiao 
et al., 2018). The results showed that the highest methane production 
enhancement was achieved with an applied voltage of 1.3 V and the 
second highest with an applied voltage of 0.8 V. Our previous study 
(Xiao et al., 2018) also found that the enhancement effect at 0.8 V was 
lower than that at 1.3 V. The change in soluble DNA of digestate in the 
four MEC-ADs (Fig. S2) showed that the applied voltage as 1.6 V cause 
certain microbial damage (Xiao et al., 2015). Meanwhile, the SEM of 
digestate at the end of AD showed that the surface of microorganisms 
was rougher at the applied voltage of 1.6 V than others (Fig. S3), also 
indicating microbial damage occurrence. Therefore, the methane pro­
duction of MEC-AD with 1.6 V was lower than those with 0.8 V and 1.3 V 
was owing to 1.6 V causing a certain microbial damage and lowering the 
microbial activity (including bacteria and archaea) (Chen et al., 2016). 
The applied voltages also increased the methane content of biogas, with 
1.6 V having the highest increase (Fig. 1-B). Water or other matter 
electrolysis might occur in the digesters at 1.3 V and 1.6 V to produce 
hydrogen and oxygen because they exceeded the lowest water elec­
trolysis voltage (Chen et al., 2016). Hydrogen would be produced in the 
digesters at 1.3 V and 1.6 V with the digester at 1.6 V producing more. 
The produced hydrogen was converted into methane by hydro­
genotrophic methanogens, which decreased the content of CO2 and 
increased that of methane. However, no oxygen or hydrogen was 
detected in the biogas, suggesting that they were rapidly consumed by 
the microorganisms (Bao et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2021). Some aerobic 
and facultative anaerobic microorganisms can grow in AD (Toerien, 
1967), and use oxygen produced by water electrolysis. Additionally, 
many microorganisms can use hydrogen in MEC-AD, which explains the 
absence of hydrogen (Guo et al., 2013; Hassanein et al., 2017). 
In addition to producing methane as energy, another important 
function of AD is organic matter removal. The removal of sludge VS and 
TCOD for the four MEC-ADs at the end of the test are summarized in 
Table 2. The VS and TCOD removal for the four MEC-ADs ranged from 
37.99% to 52.72% and 29.50%–45.05%, respectively (Table 2). The 
digester at the 1.3 V applied voltage had the highest organic matter 
removal and that at 0 V had the lowest. The results showed that the 
applied voltage increased the organic matter removal for the AD of 
sewage sludge by (11.13–38.77%), and the increase was consistent with 
their cumulative methane production (Fig. 1-A). This was logical 
because the removed organic matter was mainly converted into methane 
during AD (Xiao et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2020). 
3.2. Production of hydrogen sulfide 
H2S is a harmful component of biogas produced in sludge AD 
(Krayzelova et al., 2015) (Fig. 1-C and D). The H2S content of biogas for 
the four MEC-ADs at the end of the test was 0.302 ± 0.009% (0 V), 0.239 
± 0.008% (0.8 V), 0.005 ± 0.000% (1.3 V), and 0.001 ± 0.000% (1.6 V) 
(Fig. 1-D), which suggests that the applied voltages decreased the H2S 
content of biogas. At the end of the test, the H2S produced in MEC-AD at 
0.8 V (0.568 ± 0.019 mL) was slightly lower than that at 0 V (0.571 ±
0.017 mL) (Fig. 1-C). H2S produced in the MEC-ADs at 1.3 V (0.030 ±
0.001 mL) and 1.6 V (0.011 ± 0.000 mL) (Fig. 1-C) was far lower than 
the production at 0 V. The results showed that the H2S production in the 
MEC-AD reduced with an increase in applied voltage (94.8–98.2%) and 
the 1.6 V had the highest reduction. The AD of sulfur-containing com­
pounds in sewage sludge produces H2S (Krayzelova et al., 2015; Nguyen 
et al., 2018). The low H2S content of the biogas produced from MEC-ADs 
at 1.3 V and 1.6 V indicated that the reduction of sulfur-containing 
compounds may have stopped or that H2S may be converted further 
(Krayzelova et al., 2015; Nguyen et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2020). 
The sulfate (SO4
2−) concentration in the digestate was measured at 
the start and end of the test (Table 3). The result showed that the sulfate 
concentrations were below the detection limit in the start and end 
samples for MEC-ADs at 0 V and 0.8 V, and were 1.613 ± 0.111 and 
8.017 ± 0.184 mg/L for the MEC-ADs at 1.3 V and 1.6 V, respectively 
(Table 3). The results showed that sulfate production occurred in the 
MEC-ADs at 1.3 V and 1.6 V. Elemental sulfur can be seen on the surface 
of digestate and electrode for the MEC-ADs at 1.3 V and 1.6 V (Fig. S4), 
which was confirmed by elemental analysis. No elemental sulfur was

and 0.8 V (Fig. S4). The result suggested that elemental sulfur was 
produced in the MEC-ADs at 1.3 V and 1.6 V (Wang et al., 2020; Luo

Therefore, the conversion of sulfur in the MEC-ADs includes the 
following processes:  
1) Reduction of inorganic and organic sulfur-containing compounds, 
which produces H2S (Mahdy et al., 2020; Nguyen and Khanal, 2018).  
2) Oxidation of H2S, which produces elemental sulfur (Eq. (1)). The 
oxygen produced in the anode diffuses into the cathode, providing

2022). SOB also could convert H2S into produce elemental sulfur 
under a limited oxygen supply (Haosagul et al., 2020). Additionally, 
H2S could also be directly oxidized into elemental sulfur on the 
anode (Eq. (2)) (Grgicak et al., 2008).

Only the first process occurred in the MEC-ADs at 0 V and 0.8 V, 
while all three processes occurred in those at 1.3 V and 1.6 V. More 
elemental sulfur oxidized to sulfate in the MEC-AD at 1.6 V than that at 
1.3 V. Therefore, MEC-ADs at 1.3 V and 1.6 V reduced H2S production as 
more H2S was oxidized. 
3.3. Changes in the ORP of digestates 
The ORP is an important parameter for microaerobic conditions (Liu 
et al., 2013; Nguyen and Khanal, 2018; Wu et al., 2021; Muller et al., 
2022), and the changes in the ORP of digestates in the digesters are 
summarized in Fig. 2. The results showed that the ORP of digestates in 
the MEC-ADs at 0 V and 0.8 V were similar, which increased from −285 
± −8 mv and −279 ± 6 mv to −424 ± −12 mv and −423 ± −13 mv 
during the test, respectively. The ORP of digestates in the MEC-ADs at 
1.3 V and 1.6 V decreased from −280 ± −6 mv and −286 ± −12 mv to 
−232 ± −7 mv and −180 ± −8 mv, respectively. The results showed 
that the digesters at 0 V and 0.8 V were anaerobic conditions and those 
at 1.3 V and 1.6 V were microaerobic conditions (Nguyen and Khanal, 
2018), that is, the applied voltages of 1.3 V and 1.6 V created micro­
aerobic conditions for MEC-AD. The result indicated that oxide (oxygen) 
might produce in the MEC-AD at 1.3 V and 1.6 V, which increased the 
ORP of digestate and created a microaerobic condition for the MEC-AD 
(Chen et al., 2016; Tartakovsky et al., 2011). There are several reasons 
for why the increasing oxidation-reduction potential could enhance 
methanization in microaerobic condition: 1) facultative anaerobes (hy­
drolytic and acidifying bacteria) can rapidly consume the dissolved 
oxygen; 2) the microorganisms in the MEC-AD form microbial aggre­
gates and methanogens are enveloped in the aggregates; 3) hydrolysis 
and acidification are enhanced in microaerobic condition, which

provide more substrates to methanogens; 4) some methanogens can 
tolerate oxygen exposure (Fu et al., 2023). Therefore the microaerobic 
conditions in the digesters at 1.3 V and 1.6 V was the reason for 
enhanced AD, reduced H2S production, and increase in the sulfate 
concentration of digestates (Nguyen and Khanal, 2018; Muller et al., 
2022). The ORP of digestate in the MEC-AD at 1.6 V was higher than that 
at 1.3 V (Fig. 2), indicating more oxygen production (Nguyen and 
Khanal, 2018), which was the reason for higher sulfate concentration of 
digestate in the digester at 1.6 V. 
3.4. Microbial community 
3.4.1. Bacterial community 
At the phylum level, the most abundant bacterial populations were 
found to be Proteobacteria (23.64–40.13%), Chloroflexi (10.19–19.49%), 
Bacteroidetes (10.88–16.19%), and Firmicutes (8.27–7.91%) for the four 
digesters with different relative abundances at the end of the test (day 
31) (Fig. 3-A and Table S1). The results suggested that the applied 
voltage affected the bacterial community of the digestate in MEC-AD. 
These results were similar to those of studies on MEC-AD (Chen et al., 
2016) and microaeration-based AD with air or oxygen aeration (Zhuo 
et al., 2021). For example, Chen et al. (2016) found that the most 
abundant bacterial populations in the MEC-AD at 0–1.5 V applied 
voltages were Proteobacteria, Firmicutes, and Bacteroidetes for all reactors 
with different relative abundance. Zhou et al. (2021) found that Pro­
teobacteria (29.40–34.89%), Chloroflexi (13.41–21.24%), and Bacter­
oidetes (6.57–12.17%) were the dominant phyla in the digestate during 
the AD of sludge with in situ microaeration. Among these bacteria, 
Proteobacteria is the main contributor to the anaerobic fermentation 
process, including the conversion of glucose, butyrate, propionate, and 
acetate, but not for methanogenesis (Zhang et al., 2021; Mahdy et al., 
2020). Chloroflexi is responsible for the degradation of soluble microbial 
products and other complex substrates by producing hydrolytic en­
zymes, while Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes are known to include func­
tional hydrolysers and fermenters in AD, and can be promoted by 
low-oxygen range-microaeration (Zhang et al., 2021). 
SRB and SOB, two important bacteria involved in the conversion of 
sulfur (Rodrigues and Le˜ao, 2020), were analyzed, and their relative 
abundances at the genus level are summarized in Fig. 3-B, C and 
Table S2. There were 8 SRB (relative abundance >0.03%) and 9 SOB in 
the digestates. The relative abundance of SRB in the digestates at 1.3 V 
and 1.6 V (0.33% and 0.36%, respectively) was lower than that at 0 V 
and 0.8 V (1.24% and 1.18%, respectively), with that at 0 V being the 
highest. The results for the SOB were contrary to those for the SRBs 
(Fig. 3-B and C). The relative abundance of SOB in the digestates 
increased with the applied voltage. The digestate at 1.6 V had the 
highest relative abundance of SOB (0.42%) and that at 0 V had the 
lowest (0.11%) (Fig. 3-C and Table S2). The results showed that a high 
applied voltage decreased the abundance of SRB and increased the 
abundance of SOB. The different abundances of SRB and SOB were 
consistent with the production of H2S and sulfate (Fig. 1-C and Table 3). 
In the digestates, the dominant SRB and SOB were Desulfobulbus, 
Desulfovibrio, and Thiobacillus (Fig. 3-B and C). Desulfobulbus and 
Desulfovibrio are two common SRB found in AD with microaeration, 
which have been found to utilize ethanol, lactate, and hydrogen as 
electron donors and sulfate as electron acceptors to produce acetate 
(incompletely oxidizing SRB) (Liu et al., 2018; Mahdy et al., 2020; Wu 
et al., 2018). Thiobacillus is the most common SOB species found in the 
oxidation of sulfide (Krayzelova et al., 2015; Nguyen and Khanal, 2018). 
3.4.2. Archaeal community 
The archaeal communities of the inoculum and digestates for the 
four digesters at the end of the test (day 31) at the genus level are 
summarized in Fig. 4-A and Table S3. The results showed that the 
archaeal communities of the digestate were also affected by applied 
voltage. In the inoculum, the dominant archaea were Methanosaeta and 
Methanobacterium, with relative abundances of 67.53% and 22.01%, 
respectively. At the end of the test, significant changes were observed in 
the archaeal communities. In the MEC-AD at 0 V, the dominant archaea 
of digestate were Methanosarcina (47.99%) and Methanobacterium 
(32.91%). Unlike MEC-AD at 0 V, Methanobacterium became the domi­
nant archaea (78.10–96.70%) in the three digesters with applied voltage 
at the end of the test, with MEC-AD at 1.6 V having the lowest abun­
dance (Fig. 4-A). 
There are four methanogenesis pathways: hydrogenotrophic, aceto­
clastic, methylotrophic, and versatile methanogenesis (Xiao et al., 
2020). The methanogenesis pathways differed among the four digesters: 
hydrogenotrophic + acetoclastic methanogenesis for the digester at 0 V, 
and hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis for others (Fig. 4-B). These re­
sults suggest that MEC enhanced hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis, 
which is consistent with the findings of previous studies (Asztalos and 
Kim, 2015; Chen et al., 2016). However, the archaeal communities in 
this study differed from those of studies on microaeration-based AD with 
oxygen or air aeration (Fu et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2021). For example, 
Zhou et al. (2021) found that in situ microaeration by air injection 
significantly enriched acetoclastic methanogens, rather than hydro­
genotrophic methanogens. This difference may be due to the different 
microaeration methods used. Microaeration by air or oxygen injection 
only supplied oxygen or oxygen, nitrogen, and other trace gases, while 
microbial electrolysis at a high applied voltage (1.3 V and 1.6 V) used in 
this study simultaneously supplied O2 and H2 (Girotto et al., 2018; Tice 
and Kim, 2014). The hydrogen produced by electrolysis enhances the 
growth of hydrogenotrophic methanogens (Methanobacterium) (Hassa­
nein et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2016). Additionally, the relative abun­
dance of Methanobacterium in the digester at 1.6 V (78.10%) was lower 
than that in the digesters at 0.8 V and 1.3 V (95.43% and 95.58%, 
respectively) and that of Methanosarcina showed the opposite trend 
(Fig. 4-A), which may be due to the different oxygen sensitivity (Guo 
et al., 2021; Fu et al., 2016). 
4. Conclusions 
Applied voltages of 1.3 V and 1.6 V simultaneously reduced the H2S 
production (by 94.8–98.2%) and enhanced methane production (by 
12.70–57.02%) and organic matter removal (by 37.99–52.72% for VS) 
for the AD of sewage sludge. The two voltages electrolyzed water, 
increased the ORP of the digestate, and created microaerobic conditions. 
Sulfur reduction, H2S oxidation, and elemental sulfur oxidation 
occurred in AD at 1.3 V and 1.6 V. The abundance of SOB increased and 
that of SRB decreased with an increase in the applied voltage. ADs at the 
two applied voltage enhanced the growth of Methanobacterium.
